introduction-when-cache-becomes-database.core: MemoryDB is a Redis/Valkey-compatible, durable in-memory database: every write is committed to a Multi-AZ transaction log before acknowledgement, so data survives node failures. It offers microsecond reads and single-digit-ms writes, letting you use Redis as a primary database rather than a cache.

first_principles.problem: Teams use Redis as their primary store for sessions, carts or leaderboards, and lose data on failover with async replication.
truths: Async replication can lose recent writes.
Some workloads need both speed and durability.
Durable logs make memory stores safe.
derivation: Use **MemoryDB** when Redis data is the **source of truth**.

analogy.title: A whiteboard with an automatic notary
analogy.story: You still write quickly on the board, but every line is notarised in a ledger before you move on.
analogy.breaks: Notaries are slow; the log adds only a few milliseconds.

example.title: Shopping cart store
flow: Carts must not vanish on failover
ElastiCache async replicas could lose last writes
example.outcome: Redis as a trustworthy primary store.

check.a: Writes are committed to a distributed Multi-AZ transaction log before being acknowledged.

durability-architecture-the-transaction-.core: MemoryDB's primary applies writes in memory and synchronously appends them to a distributed transaction log replicated across multiple AZs. Only after the log confirms does the client get an OK. Replicas consume the log to stay current, and recovery replays the log, so no acknowledged write is lost.

first_principles.problem: Redis AOF/RDB on a single node can lose data if the node and disk fail together.
truths: A log replicated across AZs survives node and AZ loss.
Replicas can rebuild from the log.
derivation: **Consistency**: strong on primary, eventual on replicas.

analogy.title: A ship's logbook copied to three shore stations in real time
analogy.story: Even if the ship sinks, every recorded entry exists ashore.
analogy.breaks: Radio copies can be garbled; the log uses consensus to guarantee identical copies.

example.title: Write timeline
flow: Log append replicated across AZs (~2–5 ms)

check.q: Are reads from MemoryDB replicas strongly consistent?
check.a: No; replica reads are eventually consistent, while primary reads are strongly consistent.

memorydb-vs-elasticache-the-decision-mat.core: Choose ElastiCache for caching where data can be rebuilt: lowest write latency, cheaper and with data tiering options. Choose MemoryDB when Redis holds primary data that must survive failures: durable writes, strong consistency on the primary and simplified architecture (no separate database). Cost and write latency are higher with MemoryDB.

first_principles.problem: A team runs ElastiCache plus a database just to make session data durable, adding sync complexity.
truths: Fewer data stores mean simpler systems.

analogy.title: Sticky notes versus a bound notebook
analogy.story: Sticky notes are quick and disposable; the notebook keeps records safe.
analogy.breaks: Both tools write at almost the same speed; the difference is what survives failure.

example.title: Three workloads
flow: Game leaderboards as source of truth → MemoryDB

steps.label: Lesson
steps.detail: Ask: what happens if this data disappears?

check.q: What key question decides MemoryDB vs ElastiCache?
check.a: Whether the data is the source of truth that must survive failures, or re-creatable cache data.

cluster-architecture-sharding-and-replic.core: MemoryDB clusters use Redis Cluster semantics: data split across up to 500 shards by hash slot, each shard with one primary and up to five replicas spread across AZs. Scale out by adding shards (online resharding), scale reads with replicas and scale up by changing node types.

first_principles.problem: One shard can't hold or write the whole dataset fast enough.
truths: Replicas add read capacity and failover targets.
derivation: Choose **shard count** for memory and write throughput.

analogy.title: Branch libraries each with backup copies
analogy.story: Books are split among branches by title, and each branch keeps duplicate copies in nearby annexes.
analogy.breaks: Libraries lend physical books; replicas serve copies of the same data simultaneously.

check.q: How do you increase MemoryDB write throughput?
check.a: Add shards so writes are spread across more primaries.

snapshots-restore-and-disaster-recovery.core: MemoryDB takes automatic daily snapshots (retained up to 35 days) and manual snapshots, stored in S3 and copyable across regions or exportable. Restoring creates a new cluster. The transaction log already covers node and AZ failures; snapshots cover operator errors, corruption and regional DR. Multi-Region clusters add active-active replication.

first_principles.problem: A bad deploy flushes keys and the team has no point to restore from.
truths: Durability doesn't protect against bad writes.
derivation: **Restore** into a new cluster and repoint apps.

analogy.title: Daily photos of the whiteboard
analogy.story: Even if someone wipes it, you can redraw yesterday's state.
analogy.breaks: Photos are instant; restores create a new cluster, taking minutes.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Recovery point before every risky change.

code.text:
aws memorydb create-snapshot --cluster-name prod --snapshot-name pre-release-2026-10-18
aws memorydb copy-snapshot --source-snapshot-name pre-release-2026-10-18 --target-snapshot-name dr-copy --target-bucket dr-bucket

check.q: Why take snapshots if MemoryDB is already durable?
check.a: Durability protects acknowledged writes from failures, not from bad writes, deletions or regional disasters.

failover-mechanics-what-actually-happens.core: When a primary fails, MemoryDB detects it, picks a replica that's fully caught up with the transaction log, promotes it, and updates cluster topology. Because the log holds every acknowledged write, no committed data is lost. Clients see brief errors (MOVED or connection resets) and reconnect via the cluster endpoint, typically within seconds.

first_principles.problem: Teams fear failover loses data or requires manual action.
truths: A replica can catch up from the log before promotion.
derivation: Clients **retry with backoff** and refresh topology.

analogy.title: A relay team with a written race log
analogy.story: If the runner falls, the next one reads the log and continues exactly where they stopped.
analogy.breaks: Relay handoffs take a moment; clients must tolerate a few seconds of errors.

steps.label: Observe
steps.detail: Client errors for ~5–10 s, then normal; no key loss.

check.q: Why doesn't MemoryDB lose acknowledged writes on failover?
check.a: The promoted replica first catches up from the durable transaction log containing every acknowledged write.
